dataSetInformation.common:generalComment:
Notice: this data set supersedes the EF3.0-compliant version (see link under "preceding data set version" below calculated with the EF3.0). The life cycle inventory is not changed from the original EF3.0 data set. The LCIA results are calculated based on the EF3.1 methods which provide updated characterisation factors in the following impact categories: Climate Change, Ecotoxicity freshwater, Photochemical Ozone Formation, Acidification, Human Toxicity non-cancer, and Human Toxicity cancer. The review report and the data quality ratings refer to the original results. The data set has been updated by the European Commission on the basis of the original EF3.0 data set delivered by the data provider.This dataset represents the production of 1 m2 of finished leather in Europe by high environmental practice tanneries, with a density of 1.5 kg/m2 finished leather. It is an adjustment of the base model used for the leather datasets using information shared by COTANCE, the Best Available Techniques (BAT) Reference Document for the Tanning of Hides and Skins, and from the 2020 EU Leather Industry Social & Environmental Report. Veal and reptile leathers are not considered.
EU Leather Industry Social & Environmental Report 2020 is based on data collected annually from 79 companies (5% of the EU total) from Italy, Germany, Austria, Denmark, Sweden, UK, Spain, France, Portugal, Hungary and Romania), covering 43% of total EU leather production. Reference period: 2016 - 2018 (inclusive), with some data from 2012 and 2020.
# Differences from typical production and best practice tanneries in the EU: 1. Water usage: 120 m3 / m2 leather, compared with 148 m3 /m2 finished leather. Former value based on EU Leather Industry Social & Environmental Report 2020, average 2016-18 2. Water treatment: Values of treatment efficiency are replaced with those from EU Leather Industry Social & Environmental Report 2020 (COTANCE and industriAll-Europe, 2020), and compared with water emissions measured after treatment from two treatment plant reports from Italy (Cuiodepur and Acque del Chiampo) 3. Total Primary Energy = 73.7 MJ/m2, and shares of each energy source updated, also from the the EU Leather SER 2020.
# Weighting of different leather types: 1. Market shares for each animal leather type based on Table 4, UNIDO. ‘Future Trends in the World Leather and Leather Products Industry and Trade’, 2010. https://leatherpanel.org/sites/default/files/publications-attachments/future_trends_in_the_world_leather_and_leather_products_industry_and_trade.pdf. This data originally comes from the FAO. Market shares for each animal leather type are as follows: market_share_cattle: 66% market_share_sheep: 15% market_share_pig: 11% market_share_goat: 7% market_share_other (reptile, etc): 1% Bovine leather is predominantly (approx. 90%, Leather PEFCR) from adult cattle, so veal leather is not modelled. Reptile leather is also not included as it has a market share of less than 1%, and the models has a low data quality. Input of the pig hide is not included as there is zero allocation of the environmental impact of slaughter to the pig hide
2. Proportion of leather tanned by each technique based on Table 7, p.8 and Annex 5, De Rosa-Giglio, Fontanella, Gonzalez-Quijano, Ioannidis, Nucci, and Brugnoli. ‘PRODUCT ENVIRONMENTAL FOOTPRINT CATEGORY RULES Leather’, 25 April 2018. It is assumed that chrome-free (12% market share) refers to wet-white (and not vegetable, which is a separate category), and wet-white metal-free and wet-white metal tanning each contribute 50% of this tanning technique
# Energy Total primary energy = 1.76 tonnes oil equivalent / m2 finished leather = 73.7 MJ/m2 Share for each energy fraction based on p.26 of EU Leather Social and Environmental Report 2020. total_primary_energy_per_m2 * proportion_energy_type
Source: p.25 COTANCE and IndustriAll-Europe, 2020, SER 2020.
# Conversion factors Sources reporting values per tonne raw hide, are converted from mass per tonne raw hide to per m2 using conversion factor of kg_hide_per_m2_leather = 6.3 (default) based on Table 7, p.8 and Annex 5, Leather PEFCR, 2018. Average weighted by end-use and proportion of animal type in each end use. This is a parameter that can be adjusted if the value is known
Density of 1.50 kg/m2 averaged across different leather types is based on Thanikaivelan, Shelly, and Ramkumar, ‘Gauge Length Effect on the Tensile Properties of Leather’.; Pati, Chaudhary, and Subramani, ‘Biochemical Method for Extraction and Reuse of Protein and Chromium from Chrome Leather Shavings’.; Clarke, ‘Some Density Data on Leather’.; Dilek et al., ‘Evaluation of Collagen Hydrolysate on the Performance Properties of DifferentWet-White Tanned Leathers’.; BASF, 2003; COTANCE, 2021, personal communications; De Rosa-Giglio et al., ‘PRODUCT ENVIRONMENTAL FOOTPRINT CATEGORY RULES Leather’.; Andrea Fontanella et al., ‘Leather PEF Screening Report in the Context of the EU Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCR) Pilots’.
Note that density depends on whether full-grain (with the more dense corium layer) or split-grain (without) leathers are used.
# Waste Water and Emissions Waste water is used to balance the mass in the model. Emissions are averaged from a mix of tanning techniques and regions, see comments on the exchanges for the sources used for each emission.
Mass waste water = Mass of inputs – mass of leather out – mass of emissions (to water and air) – mass of textile machinery where Mass of leather = density of leather (kg/m3) × thickness of leather (m) × area leather (m2) The proportion of tanning agents and other synthetic compounds being absorbed into the final leather or being emitted into the water stream cannot be determined in general from the data used, and varies strongly based on the tannery parameters.

technology.technologyDescriptionAndIncludedProcesse:
System boundaries: The dataset describes the tanning and finishing of cattle leather. The inventory includes the following flows: - Electricity and heat use - Chemicals: chromium tanning agent, wetting agents, liming agents, fatliquors and other agents used in the processing of leather - Water - Emissions to water - Transport of chemicals, and raw materials
It does not include: - Packaging materials - Certain chemicals have been replaced with proxies where there is no exact match - Animal leathers for which market share is less than 1% (reptile)

LCIMethodAndAllocation.deviationsFromLCIMethodPrinciple: The background data uses: - the \xe2\x80\x9cRecycled content cut-off\xe2\x80\x9d approach to allocate end-of-life by-products and secondary materials. This allocation is explained in the description of the recycled content system model (http://www.ecoinvent.org/database/system-models-in-ecoinvent-3/cut-off-system-model/allocation-cut-off-by-classification.html). OR - EF compliant data
LCIMethodAndAllocation.deviationsFromLCIMethodApproaches: Background data: - the \xe2\x80\x9cRecycled content cut-off\xe2\x80\x9d approach to allocate end-of-life by-products and secondary materials. This allocation is explained in the description of the recycled content system model (http://www.ecoinvent.org/database/system-models-in-ecoinvent-3/cut-off-system-model/allocation-cut-off-by-classification.html). The ecoinvent database mostly relies on “Allocation – market values” apart for few exceptions particularly in the energy sector. ecoinvent energy data is replaced with EF3.0 core data as per the EF guidelines version 2.0. OR - EF compliant data
LCIMethodAndAllocation.modellingConstants: All modelling constants follow the requirements listed in the Tender Specifications 070201/2020/SER/ENV.B1. Completeness: There are no intentional cut-offs in the inventory no matter how small their contribution to all the EF impact categories is. Eventual cut-offs are in compliance with the Guide for EF compliant data sets (JRC 2020), i.e. only if below the 3% cut-off rule. Water use: water use is modelled at country level using separate flows for water withdrawal, water release and water evaporation. Handling multi-functional processes: the following PEF multi- functionality decision hierarchy is applied for resolving all multi- functionality problems: (1) subdivision or system expansion; (2) allocation based on a relevant underlying physical relationship (substitution may apply here); (3) allocation based on some other relationship. Direct land use change: GHG emissions from direct LUC allocated to good/service for 20 years after the LUC occurs, with IPCC default values. Carbon storage and delayed emissions: credits associated with temporary (carbon) storage or delayed emissions up to 300 years are not be considered. Emissions off-setting: are not included. Capital goods (including infrastructures) and their End of life: they are included. System boundaries: system boundaries include all processes linked to the product supply chain (e.g. maintenance). Time period: emissions and removals are modelled as if released or removed at the beginning of the assessment method. Fossil and biogenic carbon emissions and removals: removals and emissions are modelled as follows: All GHG emissions from fossil fuels (including peat and limestone) are modelled consistently with the most updated ILCD list of elementary flows. The non-fossil (biogenic) carbon flows are modelled consistently with the most updated ILCD list of elementary flows.

dataSourcesTreatmentAndRepresentativenes.dataCutOffAndCompletenessPrinciples: There are no intentional cut-offs in the inventory no matter how small their contribution to all the EF impact categories is. Eventual cut-offs are in compliance with the Guide for EF compliant data sets (JRC 2020), i.e. only if below the 3% cut-off rule. The dataset dry mass and water balance has been checked to ensure the inventory is complete. Capital goods (e.g. infrastructure) and their end-of-life are included.
dataSourcesTreatmentAndRepresentativenes.dataSelectionAndCombinationPrinciples: These datasets include, in both their foreground and background data, links to EF3.0 compliant data. The relevant background data on energy, transport, and End of Life are from the LCDN data node (http://lcdn.thinkstep.com/Node/). All other background data in the supply of this product for which no EF3.0 process was available are from ecoinvent v3.7 database (www.ecoinvent.org) or other data sources.
dataSourcesTreatmentAndRepresentativenes.dataTreatmentAndExtrapolationsPrinciples: Several data sources have been used to model the inventory.

review.common:reviewDetails: Internal reviews have been asked to review the plausibility of the unit process, LCIA scores, and DQRs. Internal reviewers have also been asked to review the data for EF compliancy. The consortium is therefore responsible for aspects such as compliancy with the ILCD format, including validation in Look@LCI, and nomenclature. Internal reviwers have been asked to judge based on the process name, that the unit process models in a complete and representative way the process in the requested location. The review encompassed the plausability of: - exchanges with nature (elementary flows) as well as exchanges such as product and waste flows. - meta information (general comment, technology comment, system boundaries, allocation, cut-off rules, etc.). Reviewers were asked to judge if the provided information is enough to understand the content of the process. - LCIA scores - DQRs including precision, technology, time and geography. As well as the overall DQR.

External reviewers have been asked to provide their expertise in the field of interest. External reviewers have been asked to review the unit process, including eventual methodological choices, the LCIA scores (provided with contribution scores as well), and DQRs. External reviewers have been provided all the information in a tool developed by the consortium for the purpose of this project. External reviewers have been asked to judge based on the process name, that the unit process models in a complete and representative way the process in the requested location. The review encompassed: - Plausability and completeness of exchanges with nature (elementary flows) as well as exchanges such as product and waste flows. - Review of meta information (general comment, technology comment, system boundaries, allocation, cut-off rules, etc.). Reviewers were asked to judge if the provided information is enough to understand the content of the process. - Review of properties (biogenic carbon and water content). - Review of allocation keys. - Plausability of LCIA scores calculated by the consortium. - Plausability of DQRs including precision, technology, time and geography. As well as the overall DQR.
